article.title: How to judge an election model
article.subtitle: What would it mean for FLIPR to have a bad night? Plus, more on Haley Stevens and those NYT polls in Still Counting EP9.

extraction.summary: Pre-election essay on how to evaluate a probabilistic model, and a list of candidate FLIPR changes written down in advance. The four criteria are: calibration on true out-of-sample predictions, not backtests; whether the model would have made money against markets and consensus; proportional, directionally sensible responses to new evidence; and whether it was lucky or good, tested through its structural hypotheses and margins, not just calls. Silver reports that the 18-year FiveThirtyEight/Silver Bulletin record shows sports forecasts very well calibrated and politics forecasts slightly underconfident. He lists ten possible FLIPR changes and notes they lean roughly evenly between the parties.

findings.statement: Probabilistic forecasts should be judged by calibration over a large sample of true out-of-sample predictions; for example, of 100 events forecast at 30 percent, 27 to 34 occurring is good. Backtesting does not count, since any competent model fits past data and may be overfit. Silver considers bragging about backtested results a negative sign compared with explaining why a model makes structural sense.
findings.rationale: Overfitting to random features of past data.

findings.statement: Over the 18-year FiveThirtyEight/Silver Bulletin track record of published out-of-sample forecasts, sports forecasts were extremely well-calibrated, while politics forecasts were well-calibrated but somewhat underconfident, with too few upsets relative to model expectations. Significance is hard to assess because polling errors are correlated across states.
findings.evidence_quote: Our politics forecasts were pretty well-calibrated too, although actually a bit underconfident: there were actually too few upsets relative to what our models expected.

findings.statement: Calibration alone is insufficient: a model forecasting everything at 50/50 is perfectly calibrated but useless, so discrimination (e.g. Brier score) also matters. Under a Bayesian view, a very low-probability event occurring (e.g. 0.03 percent) is much more damaging to a model than a 30 percent event.
findings.evidence_quote: A 0.03 percent chance happening is much more suspect for your model than a 30 percent hitting.

findings.statement: A model can also be judged by whether betting on it would have made money against markets and consensus. In 2016, with FiveThirtyEight giving Trump about 1 in 3 and markets offering 5-1 or 6-1, the model implied a large Trump bet. In 2026 FLIPR led Polymarket's Senate odds over time, reaching the same place faster.
findings.evidence_quote: If you trusted our model in 2016, you should actually have made a large bet on Trump

findings.statement: A well-constructed model responds proportionally, in magnitude and direction, to new evidence. For example, a set of very strong NYT/Siena polls raised Democratic Senate odds about 2 points, reasonable because odds were already favorable and NYT/Siena was expected to lean somewhat Democratic.

quantities.name: Senate odds change from NYT/Siena batch

findings.evidence_quote: The third thing I always look at is whether a model responds proportionally to new evidence.

findings.statement: To tell luck from skill, test the model's structural hypotheses against results, for example that incumbency matters less, that midterm state errors are correlated less than in presidential years, and that governor races are less partisan. Judge margins, not just calls: a 1-point loss where the model was confident is a bad forecast even if the call was right.
findings.evidence_quote: For all of this, by the way, margins ought to matter and not just the final calls.

findings.statement: Silver's pre-registered list of possible FLIPR changes: (1) treat polling errors as persistent for specific candidates such as Collins, against which he has a strong prior; (2) a fancier undecided-voter adjustment by state lean; (3) credit WAR or past margins for non-incumbents; (4) include non-individual fundraising sources; (5) account for candidate ideology; (6) improve partisan lean for midterm versus presidential electorates, registration and migration; (7) remove the expert-ratings layer; (8) force the House popular vote estimate closer to the generic ballot, currently 1 to 1.5 points apart by design; (9) use early voting, which would be a beast; (10) de-emphasize polling generally. Changes 1, 2, 4 and 10 would likely help Republicans in 2026 and 3, 5, 8 and 9 Democrats.

quantities.name: House popular vote vs generic ballot gap

findings.rationale: Keeping a list ahead of time avoids being overly results-driven and fighting the last war.
findings.evidence_quote: I always think it’s helpful to keep a mental list of these ahead of time so you’re not too overly driven by results and wind up fighting the last war.

findings.statement: FLIPR moved slightly toward fundamentals in its 2026 rebuild but remains truer to polls than some competitors, especially for the national environment. Silver warns that models with strong fundamentals that override polls are easy to overfit and have a middling-to-poor track record.
findings.evidence_quote: models that make stronger assumptions about fundamentals and let them override polls are easy to overfit, and frankly have a middling-to-poor track record.

open_questions: Published calibration statistics for FiveThirtyEight political forecasts by probability bin.
